messages.subject: [statnet_help] question on input for dyadic attributes (edgecov and dyadcov) in ergm
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] question on input for dyadic attributes (edgecov and dyadcov) in ergm
messages.body_plain:
Hi Chanung,

It sounds like what you have is nodal attribute data (like gdp) and you 
want to model the potential impact of these on tie formation.  This is 
effectively a question about selective mixing based on nodal attributes. 
While you can think about this at the dyadic level, it really is a 
property of the (two) nodes.

Why do you want to model it as a dyadic covariate rather than a nodal 
covariate (using, for example, the absdiff ergm term)?

best,
Martina

On Mon, 30 Nov 2009, chanung park wrote:

> Hello. I have been trying to apply ergm to? a symmetric trading data between countries.
> 
> I also have a number of binary, categorical, and continuous (quantitative) dyadic
> attributes. For example, I am interested in how two countries with similar or
> different gdp would form a trading tie.
> 
> To include those continuous dyadic attributes, first, I used the following line
> for each attributes (gdp and distance):
> 
> table_gdp<-read.table("gdp.txt")
> matrix_gdp<-data.matrix(table_gdp)
> gdp<-network(matrix_gdp, directed=FALSE)
> 
> table_distance<-read.table("dist.txt")
> matrix_distance<-data.matrix(table_distance)
> distance<-network(matrix_distance, directed=FALSE)
> 
> Basically. gdp.txt is a country-by-country gdp matrix in which a cell consists
> of gdp for country 1 multiplied by gdp for country 2.
> 
> dist.txt is a country-by-country distance matrix.
> 
> However, when I included them in ergm as follows, the output shows no significant results.
> 
> model1<-ergm(trade~edges+edgecov(gdp)+edgecov(dist))
> 
> Also, instead of making dyadic attributes as network variable as above,
> I also tried to include them as matrix as follows:
> 
> table_gdp<-read.table("gdp.txt")
> matrix_gdp<-data.matrix(table_gdp)
> 
> table_distance<-read.table("dist.txt")
> matrix_distance<-data.matrix(table_distance)
> 
> model1<-ergm(trade~edges+edgecov(matrix_gdp) + edgecov(matrix_dist)).
> 
> Then, I got different results from the above input method where I made
> dyadic attributes as network instead of matrix type.
> 
> To summarize, I'd like know what is a correct method for using
> multiple continuous or quantitative dyadic attributes. Also, if a network is directed,
> can I just use dyadcov instead of edgecov, but in the same format?
> 
> Thanks.

messages.subject: [statnet_help] statnet missing from CRAN?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jim.  I didn't know statnet had been removed from CRAN.  As a  
stopgap, you can install individual packages that fall under the  
statnet umbrella.  The most commonly-used of these are network, sna,  
and ergm.  If you install these three packages from CRAN (by using the  
install.packages command exactly as you've done below), you should do  
so in that order, since ergm depends on network.  (Technically, sna  
does not, though it is written to exploit network if network is loaded.)

If there are other statnet packages that you know you want, those too  
can be installed separately, but I believe the three above are the  
most commonly-used.  In fact, the only thing that the statnet  
"package" does -- when it's working -- is to install a series of other  
CRAN packages (including the three above, of course).

Once these are installed you can type 'library(ergm)' or  
'library(network)' or 'library(sna)' to use the packages.

Dave

messages.body_plain:
It seems that the network package doesn't actually preserve valued  
relations when coercing matricies into networks. For example:

 > m <- matrix(c(0,2,2,0),nrow=2)
 > n <- network(m)
 > degree(n)
[1] 2 2
 > degree(m)
[1] 4 4

Does the network package assume that networks are not valued? Or am I  
missing something else here?

Thanks
-AHM

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Valued networks in network package
messages.body_plain:
You want to use the network.adjacency option to create a valued adjacency matrix

m = matrix(c(0,2,2,0),nrow=2)
n = network(m)
degree(n)
network.adjacency(m,n)
degree(n)
degree(m)

If you're familiar with R you'll a little confused by the syntax for
network.adjacency, where m is the adjacency matrix that defines the
values of the ties in n. The function (I think) takes care of the
assignment itself.

Hope that helps,
Sam Stewart

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Valued networks in network package
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Alex -

Alexander H. Montgomery-Amo wrote:
> It seems that the network package doesn't actually preserve valued 
> relations when coercing matricies into networks. For example:
> 
>  > m <- matrix(c(0,2,2,0),nrow=2)
>  > n <- network(m)
>  > degree(n)
> [1] 2 2
>  > degree(m)
> [1] 4 4
> 
> Does the network package assume that networks are not valued? Or am I 
> missing something else here?
> 

Network objects can contain arbitrary edge metadata (including numeric 
values).  To include this information, you need to either tell the 
network constructor how to store it, or else add it later (using, e.g., 
the %e% operator or add.edge.attribute).  Here's a simple example:

#Create a test matrix
library(sna)
library(network)
mat<-rgraph(5)*matrix(1:25,5,5)
mat

#Create a network object, storing the edge values in "value"
net<-network(mat,ignore.eval=FALSE,names.eval="value")
summary(net)

#Retrieve the original form using as.sociomatrix
all(as.sociomatrix(net,"value")==mat)

Note that, since network objects can in theory contain any number of 
edge attributes of any type (including lists, complex objects, etc.), 
most functions try not to make too many assumptions about them.  Some of 
the shortcuts (e.g., %e%) are made specifically to handle standard 
vector types (characters, numerics, etc.), but the core functions (e.g., 
add.edge.attribute) have to be able to work with much more general data 
types.  Thus one needs to specifically tell commands like network() what 
you want to do with any available metadata.

Hope that helps,

-Carter
